nodes.title: Introduction to Cognitive Science
nodes.description: A team-taught course highlighting development of the field and the broad range of topics covered in the major. Example topics include addiction, analogy, animal cognition, human-computer interaction, language, neuroimaging, neural networks, reasoning, robots, and real-world applications.

nodes.title: Introduction to Communication
nodes.description: This course is an introduction to the history, theory, and practice of communication. Topics covered include language literacy, representation, semiotics, mediated technologies, institutional formations, and social interaction. Course work may involve media production (for example, writing, video and media production, or performance). No credit for COMM 10 if taken after COMM 10R.

nodes.title: Introduction to Communication
nodes.description: This course is an introduction to the history, theory, and practice of communication. Topics covered include language literacy, representation, semiotics, mediated technologies, institutional formations, and social interaction. Course work may involve media production (for example, writing, video and media production, or performance). This is a distance education course. No credit for COMM 10R if taken after COMM 10.

nodes.title: Analysis of Audio/Visual Media: Form, Style, and Meaning
nodes.description: This course builds the critical skills to understand, analyze, interpret audio/visual media by introducing students to the basic vocabulary and grammar of audio and moving image texts—how they create meaning through compositional form and narrative style—and key critical methodologies for interpreting media culture. Concepts covered will lay the groundwork for continued study in scholarly communication areas and hands-on sound, film/video, and/or social media production. No credit for COMM 20 if taken after COMM 20R.

nodes.title: Digital Media Literacy: Analyzing Forms, Practices, and Infrastructures of Mediated Public Life
nodes.description: The role of digital communication in a democratic system, and the ways mass media both facilitate and inhibit the development of a viable public sphere. By exploring today’s digital communication dynamics, students will have the opportunity to become more mindful, active consumers of media and to feel empowered to be engaged participants in public life. No credit for COMM 30 if taken after COMM 30GS or COMM 30R.

nodes.title: Global Digital Media Literacy: Analyzing Forms, Practices, and Infrastructures of Mediated Public Life
nodes.description: This course focuses on the role of journalism in a global system, and the ways mass media both contribute to and inhibit the development of a viable public sphere and effective political process. With a focus on American as well as international news media, we will examine theories and functions of journalism as well as current issues facing today’s news producers. This is a Global Seminar course. No credit for COMM 30GS if taken after COMM 30 or COMM 30R. Program or materials fees may apply.

nodes.title: Digital Media Literacy: Analyzing Forms, Practices, and Infrastructures of Mediated Public Life
nodes.description: The role of digital communication in a democratic system, and the ways mass media both facilitate and inhibit the development of a viable public sphere. By exploring today’s digital communication dynamics, students will have the opportunity to become more mindful, active consumers of media and to feel empowered to be engaged participants in public life. This is a distance education course. No credit for COMM 30R if taken after COMM 30 or COMM 30GS.

nodes.title: Introduction to Promotional Communication
nodes.description: A critical-cultural communication introduction to fields of practice that publicize, promote, or increase awareness of brands, ideas, products, and causes. Exploration of public communication industries and practices, the pressures that shape these industries and practices, and their implications for culture and society. Course will address major promotional industries such as advertising, public relations, marketing, and social media.

nodes.title: Presenting and Public Speaking
nodes.description: This course covers the basics of communication in public and professional settings. Students will cultivate their own speaking style while developing skills in delivery, performance, and persuasion. They will learn how to create a slide deck as well as prepare for speeches, interviews, and Q and As.

nodes.title: Introduction to Environmental Justice
nodes.description: This course examines how people disproportionately impacted by environmental harms mobilize across identities including race and immigration status for environmental justice where they live, work, and play. Drawing on social movements, scientific studies, and legal cases, we will explore theories and practices of race, nature, and climate change.

nodes.title: Topics in Communication
nodes.description: Introductory study in the discipline of communication, covering foundational skills and topics in areas like culture, technology, science communication, activism, and the environment. Topic and description are determined by the instructor and provided by the department quarterly.

nodes.title: Public Presentation and Persuasion—Speech and Debate
nodes.description: Throughout history, important advances in a democratic society have emerged most often from civil, rigorous discussion, debate, and persuasion. Students develop research, critical thinking, presentation, public speaking, and argumentation skills through in-class practice speeches and debates, along with participation in intercollegiate speech and debate tournaments. May be taken for credit up to six times.

nodes.title: First-year Student Seminar
nodes.description: The First-year Student Seminar Program is designed to provide new students with the opportunity to explore an intellectual topic with a faculty member in a small seminar setting. First-year student seminars are offered in all campus departments and undergraduate colleges, and topics vary from quarter to quarter. Enrollment is limited to fifteen to twenty students, with preference given to entering first-year students.

nodes.title: Communication, the Person, and Everyday Life
nodes.description: This course is a critical introduction to processes of interaction within lived and built environments. It includes historical survey of theories and methods including actor network-theory, conversation analysis, ethnography, ethnomethodology, cultural linguistics, performance, and social cognition. Course work may integrate scholarly study with production (for example, in-context observation and research or audio/video production). No credit for COMM 100A if taken after COMM 100AR.

nodes.title: Communication, the Person, and Everyday Life
nodes.description: This course is a critical introduction to processes of interaction within lived and built environments. It includes historical survey of theories and methods including actor network-theory, conversation analysis, ethnography, ethnomethodology, cultural linguistics, performance, and social cognition. Course work may integrate scholarly study with production (for example, in-context observation and research or audio/video production). This is a distance education course. No credit for COMM 100AR if taken after COMM 100A.

nodes.title: Communication, Culture, and Representation
nodes.description: This course is a critical introduction to the history of representation, surveying a range of theories and methods that have been used to understand and shape representational practices. The course will focus on relationships between form and content across various representational genres in shifting cultural contexts. Course work may integrate scholarly study with production (e.g., image-making or video/media production). No credit for COMM 100BR if taken after COMM 100B.

nodes.title: Communication, Culture, and Representation
nodes.description: This course is a critical introduction to the history of representation, surveying a range of theories and methods that have been used to understand and shape representational practices. The course will focus on relationships between form and content across various representational genres in shifting cultural contexts. Course work may integrate scholarly study with production (e.g., image-making or video/media production). This is a distance education course. No credit for COMM 100B if taken after COMM 100BR.

nodes.title: Communication, Institutions, and Power
nodes.description: This course is a critical introduction to structures of communication formed at the intersection of the state, the economy, and civil society. It includes a historical survey of communication and media industries; legal and policy-based arenas; and civic, political, and social organizations. Students will learn to assess the movement of power through these institutions and its effect in shaping society, culture, and politics. No credit for COMM 100C if taken after COMM 100CR.

nodes.title: Communication, Institutions, and Power
nodes.description: This course is a critical introduction to structures of communication formed at the intersection of the state, the economy, and civil society. It includes a historical survey of communication and media industries; legal and policy-based arenas; and civic, political, and social organizations. Students will learn to assess the movement of power through these institutions and its effect in shaping society, culture, and politics. This is a distance education course. No credit for COMM 100CR if taken after COMM 100C.

nodes.title: Introduction to Audiovisual Media Practices
nodes.description: This upper-division course is required as the gateway to all future communication media production courses. Students will learn about contemporary media practices such as film, video, digital/online, and social media production, and how these practices are formed by technical and social constraints. In the studio portion of this course, students will work hands-on with video and new media equipment to apply what they have learned.

nodes.title: Production of Activist Media
nodes.prereq_text: COMM 10 or COMM 20 or COMM 30 or COMM 30GS or COMM 40 and COMM 101.
nodes.description: In this course, we ask what techniques, strategies, and platforms we might engage to present messages in an impactful and ethical way. We engage with different media forms each quarter, maintaining an emphasis on production and documentary storytelling. The aim of this class is to demystify the idea of a “media activist” by guiding students through the development of their own media activism.

nodes.title: MPL: Nonlinear/Digital Editing
nodes.description: This hands-on post-production course introduces students to the art and practice of editing. Approaches to montage will be analyzed, discussed, and critically applied. This course is project-intensive, and will prepare students to edit using digital non-linear editing systems. May be taken for credit three times.

nodes.title: MPL: Ethnographic Methods for Media Production
nodes.description: This is a practical course on ethnographic fieldwork—obtaining informed consent, interviewing, negotiating, formulating a research topic, finding relevant literature, writing a research paper, and assisting others with their research. May be taken for credit three times.

nodes.title: MPL: Documentary Sketchbook
nodes.description: Digital video is the medium used in this class both as a production technology and as a device to explore the theory and practice of documentary production. Technical demonstrations, lectures, production exercises, and readings will emphasize the interrelation between production values and ethics, problems of representation, and documentary history. May be taken for credit three times.

nodes.title: MPL: Communication and Computers
nodes.description: This course introduces students to computers as media of communication. Each quarter, students participate in a variety of networking activities designed to show the interactive potential of the medium. Fieldwork designed to teach basic methods is combined with readings designed to build a deeper theoretical understanding of computer-based communication.

nodes.title: MPL: Sound Production and Manipulation
nodes.description: This hands-on course serves as an introduction to sound production, design, and editing. Students create projects by recording original sounds and editing on a digital audio workstation. We consider the potential of sound in film, radio, TV, and on the web by reviewing work and reading sound theory. May be taken for credit three times.

nodes.title: MPL: Topics in Production
nodes.prereq_text: COMM 101 or COGN 22 or VIS 70N prerequisites can be taken concurrently by permission.
nodes.description: Specialized study in production with topics to be determined by the instructor for any given quarter. Students will use audio/film studios, editing rooms, and cameras to produce media work in a variety of forms for various presentation platforms that can include documentary shorts, radio plays, or digital images. May be taken for credit three times.

nodes.title: MMPP: Audio Story and Podcasting Practicum
nodes.description: Production-oriented course involving diverse audio media forms. Critically analyze journalistic podcasts, features, documentaries, diaries, place-casts, and news shorts to evaluate what makes for compelling and effective audio as a contemporary storytelling form. Students will gain technical and production skills to facilitate their own creativity in the audio sphere. May be taken for credit three times.

nodes.title: MMPP: Practicum in New Media and Community Life
nodes.description: A combined lecture/lab in a specially designed after-school setting in southeastern San Diego working with children and adults. Students design new media and produce special projects, and explore issues related to human development, social justice, and community life. May be taken for credit three times.

nodes.title: MMPP: Practicum in Child Development
nodes.description: A combined lecture/lab course on after-school learning, social change, and community-based research. Students are expected to participate in a supervised after-school setting at one of four community labs in San Diego County. Students will learn ethnographic field methods, develop culturally relevant curriculum, and work in diverse settings. May be taken for credit three times.

nodes.title: MMPP: Studio Television
nodes.description: This course offers students the opportunity to produce and engage in critical discussions around various television production formats. We will study and produce a variety of projects, including public service announcements, panel programs, scripted drama, and performance productions. May be taken for credit three times.

nodes.title: MMPP: Television Analysis and Production
nodes.description: An introduction to the techniques and conventions common in television production with equal emphasis on method and content. Studio sessions provide students with opportunities to experiment in framing subject matter through a variety of cinematographic methods. May be taken for credit three times.

nodes.title: MMPP: Television Documentary
nodes.description: An advanced television course that examines the history, form, and function of the television documentary in American society. Experimentation with documentary techniques and styles requires prior knowledge of television or film production. Laboratory sessions apply theory and methods in the documentary genre via technological process. Integrates research, studio, and field experience of various media components. May be taken for credit three times.

nodes.title: CM: Documentary History and Theory
nodes.description: History of nonfiction film and video. Through film and written texts, we survey the nonfiction film genre, considering technological innovations, ethical issues, and formal movements related to these representations of the “real.”

nodes.title: CM: History of Electronic Media
nodes.description: This course considers the social, cultural, economic, and technological contexts that have shaped electronic media, from the emergence of radio and television to their convergence through the internet, and how these pervasive forms of audiovisual culture have impacted American society.

nodes.title: CMS: Asia
nodes.description: The development of media systems in Asia, focusing on India and China. Debates over nationalism, regionalism, globalization, new technologies, identity politics, censorship, privatization, and media piracy. Alignments and differences with North American and European media systems will also be considered.

nodes.title: CMS: Europe
nodes.description: The development of media systems and policies in Europe. Differences between European and American journalism. Debates over the commercialization of television. The role of media in postcommunist societies in Eastern Europe.

nodes.title: CMS: Africa
nodes.description: This course will critically examine the role of the mass media in sub-Saharan Africa in the areas of colonial rule, nationalist struggles, authoritarianism, and popular movements. It will examine general trends regionally and internationally, as well as individual national cases, from the early twentieth century to the internet news services of the information age.

nodes.title: CMS: Latin America and the Caribbean
nodes.description: The development of media systems and policies in Latin America and the Caribbean. Debates over dependency and cultural imperialism. The news media and the process of democratization. Development of the regional television industry.

nodes.title: CMS: Europe
nodes.description: This course focuses on analyzing media systems in Europe from a comparative perspective and sensitizes students to important differences with respect to journalistic and political cultures. Students will explore political, social, and economic factors shaping particular media systems and assess their implications for different types of political reporting.

nodes.title: CT: Video Game Studies
nodes.description: An introduction to video game studies, an interdisciplinary field that explores the cultural, artistic, educational, and social function of gaming. Examine this medium from historical, industrial, technological, theoretical, and aesthetic perspectives. Read from a wide variety of sources and engage in gameplay and narrative and visual analysis.

nodes.title: CT: Mobile Communication
nodes.description: Movement is central to our lives. This course draws on the latest research into how we travel, trade, and move. Diverse topics will be covered, including kids in cars, the New York subway, and theories of mobility.

nodes.title: CT: Photographic Technologies
nodes.description: This course examines photographic technologies as a set of instruments and practices that modern societies have developed and used to tell stories about themselves and make particular claims about truth and reality, focusing on the domains of science, policing, journalism, advertising, and self-expression.

nodes.title: Introduction to Media Industries
nodes.description: Introduction to topics that arise across various media industries, including media economics, ownership and consolidation in media, media regulation and deregulation, media technologies, creative labor, intellectual property, financialization, globalization, and ethics in media. Engage directly with current events, read recent coverage in the trade press, and learn to analyze contemporary media companies and systems. No credit for COMM 106 if taken after COMM 106R.

nodes.title: Streaming Media Industries
nodes.description: This course examines the ecosystem of streaming media from the perspective of power and political economy, focusing on the key corporations that shape our experience of it. How do corporations control the infrastructure of streaming media? How have streams, platforms, and algorithms changed our society? What is the effect of streaming media on creatives, laborers, and producers of content? What opportunities and obstacles are there in streaming media for more diversity and equality? No credit for COMM 106B if taken after COMM 106BR.

nodes.title: Streaming Media Industries
nodes.description: This course examines the ecosystem of streaming media from the perspective of power and political economy, focusing on the key corporations that shape our experience of it. How do corporations control the infrastructure of streaming media? How have streams, platforms, and algorithms changed our society? What is the effect of streaming media on creatives, laborers, and producers of content? What opportunities and obstacles are there in streaming media for more diversity and equality? This is a distance education course. No credit for COMM 106BR if taken after COMM 106B.

nodes.title: Data and AI Industries
nodes.prereq_text: COMM 10, COMM 20, COMM 30, COMM 30GS, or COMM 40.
nodes.description: Advances in AI and data science raise new and old issues about the role data plays in society. Students will learn how institutions (especially cultural industries) collect data, make predictions, and automate labor. Students will critically engage with data/AI practices and cultural representations of data/AI, discussing issues like privacy, power, bias, representation, regulation, and labor. Students will learn high-level tech concepts, but this class has no programming requirement.

nodes.title: The Film Industry
nodes.description: A study of the social organization of the film industry throughout its history. Who makes films, by what criteria, and for what audience? The changing relationships between studios, producers, directors, writers, actors, editors, censors, distributors, audience, and subject matter of the films will be explored. No credit for COMM 106F if taken after COMM 106FR.

nodes.title: The Film Industry
nodes.description: A study of the social organization of the film industry throughout its history. Who makes films, by what criteria, and for what audience? The changing relationships between studios, producers, directors, writers, actors, editors, censors, distributors, audience, and subject matter of the films will be explored. This is a distance education course. No credit for COMM 106FR if taken after COMM 106F.

nodes.title: Tourism: Global Industry and Cultural Form
nodes.description: The largest industry in the world has far-reaching cultural ramifications. We will explore tourism’s history and its contemporary cultural effects, taking the perspective of the “toured” as well as that of the tourist. No credit for COMM 106G if taken after COMM 106GR.

nodes.title: Tourism: Global Industry and Cultural Form
nodes.description: The largest industry in the world has far-reaching cultural ramifications. We will explore tourism’s history and its contemporary cultural effects, taking the perspective of the “toured” as well as that of the tourist. This is a distance education course. No credit for COMM 106GR if taken after COMM 106G.

nodes.title: Internet Industry
nodes.description: The political economy of the emergent internet industry, charted through analysis of its hardware, software, and services components. The course specifies leading trends and changing institutional outcomes by relating the internet industry to the adjoining media, telecommunications, and computer industries. No credit for COMM 106I if taken after COMM 106IR.

nodes.title: Internet Industry
nodes.description: The political economy of the emergent internet industry, charted through analysis of its hardware, software, and services components. The course specifies leading trends and changing institutional outcomes by relating the internet industry to the adjoining media, telecommunications, and computer industries. This is a distance education course. No credit for COMM 106IR if taken after COMM 106I.

nodes.title: Advertising and Society
nodes.description: Advertising as a commercial and social force. The development of advertising, branding, and consumer culture in the United States; the history and political economy of advertising in mass and digital media; semiotics and representation in advertisements; influencers, authenticity, and the monetization of self and community; subversion and rebellion within systems of advertisement and promotion. Renumbered from COMM 109D. No credit for COMM 106M if taken after COMM 106MR.

nodes.title: Advertising and Society
nodes.description: Advertising as a commercial and social force. The development of advertising, branding, and consumer culture in the United States; the history and political economy of advertising in mass and digital media; semiotics and representation in advertisements; influencers, authenticity, and the monetization of self and community; subversion and rebellion within systems of advertisement and promotion. This is a distance education course. No credit for COMM 106MR if taken after COMM 106M.

nodes.title: Journalism and the News Industry
nodes.description: Survey the development of journalism as a profession and news media as an industry and social institution. How to understand the production of news, the forces that shape social representations in the news, access to the public sphere, and approaches to the analysis of news media content. Debates about ethical issues in journalism, “objectivity” and the politics of news, and the sustainability of journalism as an institution. No credit for COMM 106N if taken after COMM 106NR.

nodes.title: Journalism and the News Industry
nodes.description: Survey the development of journalism as a profession and news media as an industry and social institution. How to understand the production of news, the forces that shape social representations in the news, access to the public sphere, and approaches to the analysis of news media content. Debates about ethical issues in journalism, “objectivity” and the politics of news, and the sustainability of journalism as an institution. This is a distance education course. No credit for COMM 106NR if taken after COMM 106N.

nodes.title: Introduction to Media Industries
nodes.description: Introduction to topics that arise across various media industries, including media economics, ownership and consolidation in media, media regulation and deregulation, media technologies, creative labor, intellectual property, financialization, globalization, and ethics in media. Engage directly with current events, read recent coverage in the trade press, and learn to analyze contemporary media companies and systems. This is a distance education course. No credit for COMM 106R if taken after COMM 106.

nodes.title: TV Industry
nodes.description: This course examines the political economy of television throughout its history. How TV is made, who is involved, how is industry organized, how does it get regulated, distributed? Consider how these answers changed over time and look at recent influences of digital technologies. No credit for COMM 106V if taken after COMM 106VR.

nodes.title: TV Industry
nodes.description: This course examines the political economy of television throughout its history. How TV is made, who is involved, how is industry organized, how does it get regulated, distributed? Consider how these answers changed over time and look at recent influences of digital technologies. This is a distance education course. No credit for COMM 106VR if taken after COMM 106V.

nodes.title: Visual Culture
nodes.description: How visual images contribute to our understanding of the world and ourselves. Theoretical approaches from media studies, art history, gender studies, and social theory will be used to analyze cultures of science, art, mass media, and everyday life.

nodes.title: POB: Introduction
nodes.description: How do political contests and debates come to be organized on and around bodies? In what sense is the natural body a sign system and how does its organization represent and reproduce cultural values, moral assumptions, social relations, and economic rationales? This course examines these and other questions through political, historical, and media analysis.

nodes.title: POB: Disability
nodes.description: Cultural and historical ways of defining and understanding disability relative to communication and assistive technologies, including the impact of digital technologies and the Americans with Disabilities Act. Course use of audiovisual texts and writings from fields including science and technology studies, and cultural studies.

nodes.title: Politics of Bodies: Gender and Biomedicine
nodes.description: This course explores the construction of gender by biomedicine, and the influence of conceptions of gender on the development of biomedicine. From challenges to binary conceptions of sex to the intersection of race and pharmaceutical development around the world, the course will examine the ways in which embodied experiences of gender, sexuality, and race have interacted with social processes of biomedicalization and pharmaceuticalization.

nodes.title: MC: History of Information
nodes.description: Even though we consider ours to be the Information Age, information has a rich history that goes back to the invention of the printing press. This history focuses on the rise of mechanical and social technologies that fostered the spread of information. Topics will include media and networks (books, telegraphy, internet), collecting and storage (archives, libraries, digital repositories), elemental units (facts, bits, noise), and application and use (reading, messaging, algorithms).

nodes.title: Propaganda and Persuasion
nodes.description: Propaganda and influence in historical and critical-cultural context. Defining propaganda and persuasion; histories of mass media censorship, state propaganda, and public relations; the production and interpretation of persuasive media messages; media representations of and narratives about persuasion and propaganda; digital technologies and networked influence. No credit for COMM 109P if taken after COMM 109PR.

nodes.title: Propaganda and Persuasion
nodes.description: Propaganda and influence in historical and critical-cultural context. Defining propaganda and persuasion; histories of mass media censorship, state propaganda, and public relations; the production and interpretation of persuasive media messages; media representations of and narratives about persuasion and propaganda; digital technologies and networked influence. This is a distance education course. No credit for COMM 109PR if taken after COMM 109P.

nodes.title: LLC: Communication in Organizations
nodes.description: Organizations are analyzed as historically evolving discursive systems of activity mediated by talk, text, and artifacts. The class covers sense making, coordinating, symbolizing, talking, negotiating, reading and writing, storytelling, joking, and visualizing in organizations. Exemplary case studies employing several complementary frameworks are used to analyze these communicative processes.

nodes.title: LLC: Communication and Community
nodes.description: This course examines forms of communication that affect people’s everyday lives. Focusing on ways that ethnic communities transmit and acquire information and interact with mainstream institutions, we examine a variety of alternative local media, including murals, graffiti, newsletters, and community radio.

nodes.title: LLC: Language and Human Communication
nodes.description: This course examines the interaction of language and culture in human communication. Beginning with language evolution, the course then discusses a broad range of human languages, including indigenous languages, sign languages, and hybrid languages spoken in urban centers.

nodes.title: LLC: Language, Thought, and Media
nodes.description: This course examines the ways in which various communicative channels mediate human action and thought. A basic premise of the course is that human thought is shaped in important ways by the communicative devices used to communicate. There is a particular emphasis on how thought develops, both historically and in the individual.

nodes.title: Texting and Talking
nodes.prereq_text: COMM 10, COMM 20, COMM 30, COMM 30GS, or COMM 40.
nodes.description: This course explores the complexities of how people use language in face-to-face and mediated contexts to participate in social interaction. Students will learn about how language and our use of it has evolved in the digital age, and how these ongoing shifts impact our daily lives.

nodes.title: CCP: Communication and Cultural Production: Introduction
nodes.description: This course examines the products of culture industries (e.g., music, television, fashion, food, landscape, architectural design) to analyze, specifically, how culture is consumed and by whom. How are spectators hailed and audiences fostered and shaped? And what is the role of audiences in fostering and shaping cultural forms and products?

nodes.title: CCP: Global Borders: Communication and Conflict
nodes.description: Across the globe, geopolitical borders are charged sites of cross-cultural communication and conflict. While borders are commonly conceived as fixed physical demarcations, in this course we will examine borders as sites of exchange, as contested boundaries where diverse actors and practices converge and diverge, and as complex historical and socio-spatial formations that call into question presumed divisions between inside/outside, us/them, human/nonhuman, and technological/ecological.

nodes.title: CCP: Cities and Politics of Space
nodes.description: This course offers an introduction to the production of urban space. Cities are produced by sociocultural shifts wrought by migration, technological changes, new forms of production, globalization, and climate change. How is the landscape or built environment of the city shaped by the combined and often contradictory forces of capital, expert knowledge, social movements, and urban dwellers?

nodes.title: CCP: Folklore and Communication
nodes.description: Folklore is characterized by particular styles, forms, and settings. Course introduces a range of folklore genres from different cultures, historical periods, oral narrative, material folk arts, dramas, rituals. Study of the relationship between expressive form and social context.

nodes.title: CCP: Popular Culture
nodes.description: This course provides an overview of developments in popular culture from the early twentieth century through present day, with analysis of historical pop culture texts. It also offers a review of theoretical work from cultural studies on the significance of pop culture.

nodes.title: CCP: Performance and Cultural Studies
nodes.description: Explores performance as a range of aesthetic conventions (theatre, film, performance art) and as a mode of experiencing and conveying cultural identity. Texts include critical writing from anthropology, psychology, linguistics, media studies, as well as film/video, play scripts, live performance.

nodes.title: CCP: Cultural Politics of Sport
nodes.description: Examine sports as play, performance, competition, an arena where there are politics, culture, power, identity struggles. Establishing the social meanings of sport, we address ethics, race, class, nation, gender, body, science, technology, entertainment industries, commerce, spectatorship, consumption, amateurism, professionalism.

nodes.title: IM: The Idea of Childhood
nodes.description: Our understanding of childhood as a stage of innocence is a modern idea. The idea of childhood has not been constant; different cultures, communities, and classes have shaped the integration of children according to their own standards. We examine the different ways that attitudes toward children have changed, how these attitudes have been connected to an understanding of the human being, and how the desires of society and parents are manifested in what they think the child should be.

nodes.title: IM: Language and Globalization
nodes.description: The interaction of language and culture in human communication. New and old languages, standard and dialect, dominant and endangered are the special focus. Selected languages as examples of how languages exist in contemporary contexts.

nodes.title: Intermediate Topics in Communication
nodes.description: Specialized study of communication topics, to be determined by the instructor, for any given quarter. May be taken for credit three times.

nodes.title: CSI: Human Rights, Communication, and Contemporary Global Justice
nodes.description: How should we as global citizens respond to the horrifying human rights abuses that saturate news headlines and social media posts? How do communication practices, the right to information, freedom of expression, and media and journalists function within the contemporary human rights regime? Examine human rights protections—against genocide, torture, enslavement, political persecution, gender violence, and climate displacement—and their violation through case studies from 1945 to the present.

nodes.title: CSI: Communication and Social Institutions: Human Rights Advocacy: Journalists, Activists and Scholars at Risk
nodes.description: How should we respond to the continued violation of human rights to exercise freedom of expression and to engage in open inquiry and social justice actions without fear of persecution? Students will gain a practical understanding of the mechanisms through which different actors fight for human rights by researching and/or participating in an international human rights advocacy campaign on behalf of a specific journalist, activist, or scholar at risk of expulsion, imprisonment, or death.

nodes.title: CSI: On Constitutions
nodes.description: Consider “constitutions” as meaning-making, world-building mechanisms and practices. Explore how constitutions work: as interpretive instruments designed to frame, organize, guide human thought, action, and systems (according to certain rules or principles often represented as divine in origin and universal in effect) and; as ongoing, dynamic interpretative processes that nevertheless congeal in objects, bodies, and social arrangements and are thus considered binding or unalterable.

nodes.title: CSI: New Media, Youth, and Democracy
nodes.description: Does “new media” deliver on its promise to expand access to public participation? We will analyze, produce, and counter narratives about media, youth, and democracy. The course should interest students who care about politics, human development, community engagement, or human computer interaction.

nodes.title: CSI: Gender, Labor, and Culture in the Global Economy
nodes.description: This course introduces students to different theories of globalization and of gender. Against this theoretical background, students critically examine the gendered (and racialized) nature of labor in the production of material, social, and cultural goods in the global economy.

nodes.title: CSI: Law, Communication, and Freedom of Expression
nodes.description: Examination of the legal framework of freedom of expression in the United States. Covers fundamentals of First Amendment law studying key cases in historical content. Prior restraint, incitement, obscenity, libel, fighting words, public forum, campaign finance, commercial speech, and hate speech are covered.

nodes.title: CSI: Gender and Science
nodes.description: This course will focus on arguments about cognitive differences between men and women in science. We will review current arguments about essential differences, historical beliefs about gender attributes and cognitive ability, and gender socialization into patterns of learning in school.

nodes.title: CSI: Media Technologies and Social Movements
nodes.description: Course explores the roles of media technologies in activist campaigns, social movements. Blending theory, historical case studies, and project-based group work, students will investigate possibilities and limitations of attempts to enroll new and old media technologies in collective efforts to make social change.

nodes.title: CSI: Food Justice
nodes.description: Examine food justice from multiple analytical and theoretical perspectives: race, class, diversity, equity, legal-institutional, business, ethical, ecological, scientific, cultural, and socio-technical. Compare political strategies of food justice organizations/movements aimed at creating healthy and sustainable food systems locally and globally.

nodes.title: CSI: Community Fieldwork
nodes.description: Specialized study in community-based and/or participatory design research with topics to be determined by the instructor, for any given quarter. Students who choose the option to do fieldwork for any given course, need to register for COMM 114K. May be taken for credit three times.

nodes.title: CSI: Communication and the Law
nodes.description: Using classic and modern texts, the course explores fundamental questions of law and political theory: What are rights and where do they come from? What is the balance between freedom and equality, between individual and common goods? These theoretical explorations are then oriented to specifically communication concerns: What is the relationship between privacy and personhood? Between free speech and democracy? Between intellectual property and efficient markets?

nodes.title: CSI: Communication and the Law: The Body in Law
nodes.description: This course concentrates on one area of law specific to the concerns of communication: the relationship between privacy, personhood, and bodily autonomy. Using a combination of legal texts, court cases, and theoretical literature, we will consider the changing nature of each dimension of this relationship as the courts have been called upon to adjudicate conflicting claims and visions in matters of reproduction, sexual identity, genetic engineering, and the commodification of body parts.

nodes.title: CSI: Public History and Museum Studies
nodes.description: This course will explore the role that “public history”—history as created for general audiences—plays in communicating cultural and national identities by examining museum exhibitions, their controversies, and how material objects mediate interpretations of the past.

nodes.title: CSI: Science Communication
nodes.description: This course examines science communication as a unique form of storytelling, identifying who does science communication, how, why, and with what impacts. Through an exploration of the social construction of scientific knowledge, the course highlights science communication’s role in democracy, power, justice, public reason, technological trajectories, university-community relations, and health activism.

nodes.title: CSI: Global Health Communication
nodes.description: Public health campaigns attempt to change behavior, slow the spread of disease, and improve the health of a population. This course takes a critical social science perspective on the production, dissemination, and impacts (intended and otherwise) of public health communication, including questions of coercion, autonomy, and perceptions of collective health and well-being.

nodes.title: Communication and the Senses
nodes.description: While we often assume that communication is something that happens only with our eyes and/or ears, every act of communication is multisensory, often involving sight and sound but also smell, touch, and taste. In this course, students will learn how to pay attention to and engage with the “other” senses beyond the visual and auditory. Interdisciplinary scholarship and empirical activities help students build a vocabulary for understanding the complexities of multisensory communication.

nodes.title: Data Science for Communication Students
nodes.prereq_text: COMM 10, COMM 20, COMM 30, COMM 30GS, or COMM 40.
nodes.description: Introduction to methods, theories, practices, and implications of applying data science methods to issues of communication, culture, media, and the digital humanities. Designed for communication, humanities, and qualitative social science majors. Students will learn how to collect, organize, analyze, and visualize data through programming in Python or R. Students will critically interrogate data science practice, discussing topics such as privacy, power, bias, interpretation, and context.

nodes.title: Journalistic Writing, Reporting, and Research
nodes.prereq_text: COMM 10, COMM 20, COMM 30, COMM 30GS, or COMM 40.
nodes.description: Introduction to the basics of journalistic writing, reporting, and research. Students will consider voice and bias and discuss the major issues facing journalists today. Opportunities to write and report in different modes and across a variety of media, may include podcasting, beat reporting, investigative journalism, multimedia features, and more.

nodes.title: Community and Ethnography: Critical and Practical Approaches to Fieldwork
nodes.description: Students will practice ethnography, a methodology often glossed as deep hanging out, that entails entering a reciprocal engagement with a community. Ethnography, however, is a fraught process infused with power differentials at every turn. This course is a hands-on, project-based opportunity for students to conduct ethnographic explorations in their global seminar site and reflect critically upon the process. We will also discuss ethnographies about our global seminar location. Program or materials fees may apply. This is a Global Seminar course. Course preauthorization is provided for students accepted in the Global Seminar Program.

nodes.title: Action Cinema
nodes.prereq_text: COMM 10, COMM 20, COMM 30, COMM 30GS, or COMM 40.
nodes.description: This course traces the history of the action film genre with particular attention to its historical contexts, its social meanings, and its longstanding popularity with audiences. Topics and issues to be covered will include early cinema and serial queens; genre and the action film as hybrid; the aesthetics of action; the 1980s and the blockbuster; action cinema and gender; the rise of the franchise and transnational cinema.

nodes.title: Comic Books as a Cultural Form
nodes.prereq_text: COMM 10, COMM 20, COMM 30, COMM 30GS, or COMM 40.
nodes.description: Comic books (as well as graphic novels, comic strips, and other sequential art) have been a globally influential form of media for more than a century. This course considers aspects of its artistic, cultural, and historical legacy, as well as comics’ role in contemporary society.

nodes.title: Television as a Cultural Form
nodes.prereq_text: COMM 10, COMM 20, COMM 30, COMM 30GS, or COMM 40.
nodes.description: How and what does television communicate? Emphasis will be on contemporary U.S. television programming, placed in comparative and historical context. Special topics may include TV genres, TV and politics, TV and other media. In-class screenings. (Renumbered from COMM 106T. Students may not receive credit for both COMM 118T and COMM 106T.)

nodes.title: Advanced Persuasion
nodes.description: This course instructs advanced strategies, tactics, and presentation skills necessary for superior performance in intercollegiate speech and debate competitions. May be taken for credit three times.

nodes.title: AMP: Social Issues in Media Production
nodes.description: Analyze forms of social issue media production, photography, audio/radio, arts, crafts, web, print zines, political documentary. Students work with several forms of media making: video, audio, web design, and a project in their chosen format.

nodes.title: AMP: Media Stereotypes
nodes.description: An examination of how the media present society’s members and activities in stereotypical formats. Reasons for and consequences of this presentation are examined. Student responsibilities will be (a) participation in measurement and analysis of stereotype presentations. (b) investigating techniques for assessing both cognitive and behavioral effects of such scripted presentations on the users of media. Students will not receive credit for COMT 105 and COMM 120M.

nodes.title: AMP: News Media Workshop
nodes.description: Designed for students working in student news organizations or off-campus internships or jobs in news, public relations, or public information. A workshop in news writing and news analysis.

nodes.title: AMP: Digital Media in Education
nodes.description: This course develops critical understanding of educational uses of digital media through firsthand experience in public educational settings, and readings/discussions of challenges, benefits, and pitfalls of educational applications of media technology. Three hours/week of fieldwork required.

nodes.title: AMP: Writing for Digital Media
nodes.description: Practice, history, and theory of writing for digital media. Text combines with images, sounds, movement, and interaction. New network technologies (email, blogs, wikis, and virtual worlds) create new audience relationships. Computational processes enable texts that are dynamically configured and more.

nodes.title: Critical Design Practice/Advanced Studio
nodes.prereq_text: COMM 10 or COGS 1 or DSGN 1 or ESYS 10 or POLI 10 or POLI 10D or USP 1.
nodes.description: This hands-on course introduces design as social and political transformation. In it, students will learn to analyze how designed objects and environments entail political assumptions and choices, working in groups to design an intervention into some aspect of collective life that concerns them. It will include a mixture of lectures and studio-based activities.

nodes.title: Critical Design Practice/Topic Studio
nodes.description: Course builds on understanding design as political activity. Group work to design quarter-long projects that explore political role of design, include design in built environments, organizations, media technologies. Deepened capacities to design in public, for publics, with publics. May be taken for credit three times.

nodes.title: Skills in Communication
nodes.description: Focused study on a skill set relevant to the field of communication, determined by the instructor. Topic and description to be provided by the department. Potential topics include professional writing, nonfiction writing, photojournalism, qualitative data analysis, community organizing, community education, and campaign management.

nodes.title: Children and Media
nodes.description: A course that analyzes the influence of media on children’s behavior and thought processes. The course takes a historical perspective, beginning with children’s print literature, encompassing movies, music, television, and computers. Students will study specific examples of media products intended for children and apply various analytic techniques, including content analysis and experimentation to these materials.

nodes.title: Problem of Voice
nodes.description: This course will explore the problem of self-expression for members of various ethnic and cultural groups. Of special interest is how writers find ways of describing themselves in the face of others’ sometimes overwhelming predilection to describe them.

nodes.title: Race, Nation, and Violence in Multicultural California
nodes.description: How does media representation of race, nation, and violence work? Taking multicultural California as our site, we will explore how social power is embedded in a variety of visual texts, and how media not only represents but also reproduces conflict.

nodes.title: Creative Labor in the Media Industries
nodes.prereq_text: COMM 10, COMM 20, COMM 30, COMM 30GS, or COMM 40.
nodes.description: This course examines work in cultural industries, combining macro-legal/economic and micro-sociological analyses of various “production cultures” where creative work happens. We will consider a cluster of concerns for creative, collaborative workers including ownership, authorship, and IP; occupational discrimination and equity; labor unions; workplace safety and oversight; recruitment, training, and worker mobility; flexible and on-demand labor markets; exploitation of creatives’ love of work.

nodes.title: Communication, Dissent, and the Formation of Social Movements
nodes.description: Emergence of dissent in different societies, and relationship of dissent to movements of protest and social change. Movements studied include media concentration, antiwar, antiglobalization, death penalty, national liberation, and labor. Survey of dissenting voices seeking to explain the relationship of ideas to collective action and outcomes.

nodes.title: Advanced Topics in Communication, Politics, and Society
nodes.description: Specialized study of communication, politics, and society with topics to be determined by the instructor for any given quarter. May be taken for credit three times.

nodes.title: Television and Citizenship
nodes.description: Television is a contested site for negotiating the rationales of inclusion and exclusion associated with citizenship and national belonging. Historical and contemporary case studies within international comparative contexts consider regulation, civil rights, cultural difference, social movements, new technologies, and globalization.

nodes.title: Media Audiences
nodes.description: Examines the complex relationship between mass media and the consumers and viewers they target. This course covers theories about audiences, reading practices of audiences, the economics of audiences, and the role of audiences in the digital era.

nodes.title: Contemporary Minority Media Makers and the Festival Experience
nodes.description: This advanced course examines, analyzes, and discusses media works by contemporary Asian American, Native American, African American, and Latina/o American filmmakers. The course does not offer a historical survey of films by minority makers but rather will operate on themes such as cultural identity, urbanization, personal relationships, gender relations, cultural retentions, and music. The course will require students to attend some off-campus screenings, especially those at area film festivals.

nodes.title: Transmedia
nodes.description: This course explores and critically analyzes the art and economics of contemporary transmedia. Transmedia is a mode of production in which a text or story unfolds across multiple media platforms. It will cover all the facets of this widespread phenomenon, including historical, aesthetic, industrial, theoretical, and practical dimensions.

nodes.title: Black Women Filmmakers
nodes.description: Students examine film and video media produced by black women filmmakers worldwide. This course will use readings from the writings of the filmmakers themselves as well as from film studies, women’s studies, literature, sociology, and history.

nodes.title: Black Women, Feminism, and Media
nodes.description: This course examines the challenges that arise in using feminist theory to understand black women’s experience in Africa and the United States. It also looks at the mass media and popular culture as arenas of black feminist struggle.

nodes.title: Examining Marvel’s Black Panther
nodes.description: This course looks at the politics of the cinema industry and the development and reception of Marvel’s blockbuster film, Black Panther. We read articles, books, and graphic novels connected to the film examining its reception, impact, and response. We dive deeper into the issues around cinematic representations of Black people with a focus on depictions of African cultures in cinema. We also consider the history and contributions of the original Black Panthers of the 1960s to worldwide cultures.

nodes.title: Cinema in Latin America
nodes.description: Analysis of the changing content and sociopolitical role in Latin America of contemporary media, including the “new cinema” movement, recent developments in film, and popular television programming, including the telenovela. Examples drawn from Mexico, Brazil, Cuba, and other countries. No credit for COMM 140 if taken after COMM 140GS.

nodes.title: Cinema in Latin America
nodes.description: This Global Seminar examines how film reflects social and political realities in Latin America and can be used as a vehicle for raising consciousness and, potentially, social change. Survey films from the late 1950s and the New Latin American Cinema until the present moment, with an emphasis on the site of the global seminar. Films that we will engage run the gamut from big budget to small independent productions, a curated diversity intended to engage students in thoughtful dialogue. This is a Global Seminar course. Program or material fee may apply. Course preauthorization is provided for students accepted in the Global Seminar Program. No credit for COMM 140GS if taken after COMM 140.

nodes.title: Film Authorship
nodes.description: This course examines film authorship by focusing on two filmmakers and exploring the many ways that films are authored and produce meaning. Students learn how to analyze a film’s production, collaboration, representation, reception, and industrial context, in order to explore broader themes and social issues such as race, class, gender, violence, and authorial responsibility. Film authors may include Spike Lee, Kathryn Bigelow, Bong Joon-ho, or Alfonso Cuarón.

nodes.title: Science Fiction
nodes.description: This course focuses on science fiction’s critical investigation of history, identity, and society across a range of media forms, including film, television, and literature. No credit for COMM 143 if taken after COMM 143R.

nodes.title: Science Fiction
nodes.description: This course focuses on science fiction’s critical investigation of history, identity, and society across a range of media forms, including film, television, and literature. This is a distance education course. No credit for COMM 143R if taken after COMM 143.

nodes.title: American Television in the 1970s
nodes.description: Course will explore the politics and culture of the 1970s through the lens of network television programming and the decade’s most provocative sitcoms, dramas, variety shows, and news features. Students will analyze television episodes and read relevant media studies scholarship.

nodes.title: History, Memory, and Popular Culture
nodes.description: What role does popular culture play in shaping and creating our shared memory of the past? The course examines diverse sources such as school textbooks, monuments, holidays and commemorations, museums, films, music, and tourist attractions.

nodes.title: Advanced Topics in Cultural Production
nodes.description: Specialized advanced study in cultural production with topics to be determined by the instructor for any given quarter. May be taken for credit three times.

nodes.title: Media Activism
nodes.prereq_text: COMM 10, COMM 20, COMM 30, COMM 30GS, or COMM 40.
nodes.description: This course explores the way artists and media-makers intervene in the public sphere and influence debates about pressing social, economic, and political problems. Looking at a range of media formats, we study and compare the tactics, strategies, and effectiveness of different approaches. This survey of political art and media is intended to stoke students’ curiosity in the local and global problems addressed and inspire students to engage in their own form of media art and activism.

nodes.title: Global Cultures of K-Pop
nodes.prereq_text: COMM 10, COMM 20, COMM 30, COMM 30GS, or COMM 40, or COMM 50.
nodes.description: Examine the sprawling, often contradictory cultural terrain of K-pop, South Korea’s multi-billion-dollar pop music industry. Consider the broad range of social and technological structures, creative practices, emotional attachments, and embedded value systems that have been cultivated by the industry across a range of geopolitical contexts. Explore different sets of issues and case studies anchored in critical concepts drawn from assigned readings, lectures, and experiential exercises.

nodes.title: Southern California in Cinema
nodes.description: This class examines the history and representation of Southern California on film. Consider the emergence of Hollywood as a defining moment in the history of Los Angeles and how film is central to the popular imagination of social life in Southern California. Examine the cinematic representation of different communities and neighborhoods and discuss topics such as car culture and regional sprawl, the beach as imagined lifestyle, and noir as regional critique.

nodes.title: The Information Age: Fact and Fiction
nodes.description: Analysis of the forces propelling the Information Age. An examination of the differential benefits and costs, and a discussion of the presentation in the general media of the Information Age.

nodes.title: News Media and Politics
nodes.prereq_text: COMM 10, COMM 20, COMM 30, COMM 30GS, or COMM 40.
nodes.description: How political journalism and political communication are embedded in and connected to technology, history, and culture. Role of journalism in a democratic system; how mass media contributes to and inhibits the development of a viable public sphere and effective political process. Theories and functions of journalism, political communication, and political participation. The web as a possible democratizing force; the changing nature of public deliberation in a pluralistic democratic system.

nodes.title: Architecture as Communication
nodes.description: This course examines how buildings, cities, towns, gardens, neighborhoods, roads, bridges, and other bits of infrastructure communicate. We consider both the materiality and language-like properties of physical things in order to understand how built environments are represented, experienced, and remembered.

nodes.title: Latinx Space, Place, and Culture
nodes.description: This diversity, equity, and inclusion course requirement approved course explores the power of place in the formation and representation of Latinx identities and communities in Southern California. It highlights past and current struggles to recuperate and sustain a sense of place for marginalized and displaced peoples against the colonization and racialization of formerly indigenous and Mexican territory. Students conduct research in various locations at the center of the cultural politics of Latinx place-making.

nodes.title: Media and Conflict Environment: Textual and Visual Representations
nodes.description: Environments of conflict, including war, generate enormous amounts of passion as well as controversy. This course examines how various forms of media represent violent conflicts, and the controversies that follow from these media representations. The aim of the course is to explore how the culture, political economy, and primary actors of media environments confront the challenge of covering various types of conflicts and the types of stories and images that emerge in the process.

nodes.title: Representations of the Israeli/Palestinian Conflict
nodes.description: The conflict between the state of Israel and the group of people known as Palestinians is arguably the most intractable conflict in the world today. This course is a critical engagement with debates about this conflict, and the different representations of these debates.

nodes.title: Tourism and Imperialism
nodes.description: This course studies tourism as a form of imperialism. It explores the industry’s role in reproducing race, gender, labor, and ecological and geographical inequalities by looking at real case scenarios from around the world. Traveling for pleasure is a privilege. For some to be able to travel, others need to stay still, working to accommodate tourists’ desires and consumption fantasies. The course offers critical tools to help us think about the future of tourism in the face of contemporary crises.

nodes.title: Political Economy and International Communication
nodes.description: The character and forms of international communications. Emerging structures of international communications. The United States as the foremost international communicator. Differential impacts of the free flow of information and the unequal roles and needs of developed and developing economies in international communications.

nodes.title: Advanced Studies in Cultural Industries
nodes.description: We examine how people interact with products of popular culture, production of cultural goods by looking at conditions in cultural industries. We examine film, music, publishing, focusing on how production is organized, what kind of working conditions arise, how products are distributed.

nodes.title: Concepts of Freedom
nodes.description: This course examines some of the changing cultural, social, technological, and political meanings; practices; and aspirations that together constitute what is and has been called freedom.

nodes.title: Behind the Internet: Invisible Geographies of Power and Inequality
nodes.description: This course aims to unveil the vast and largely hidden infrastructures silently shaping how digital communication take place in contemporary societies as well as the visible and invisible geographic of power and inequality these infrastructures are helping to create.

nodes.title: Surveillance, Media, and the Risk Society
nodes.description: Contributions of the field of communication to the study of surveillance and risk. Critical and legal perspectives on consumer research, copyright enforcement, the surveillance capacity of Information and Communication Technologies (ICTs), closed-circuit television, interactive media, and the “rhetorics of surveillance” in television and film.

nodes.title: Bilingual Communication
nodes.description: This course is designed to introduce students to multiple settings where bilingualism is the mode of communication. Examination of how such settings are socially constructed and culturally based. Language policy, bilingual education, and linguistic minorities, as well as field activities included.

nodes.title: Biography and Life Stories
nodes.description: Course examines several different ways of telling stories as a form of communication: our own life and about the lives of others. There are also the occasions that the life stories of ordinary people are told at and celebrated, for example, funerals, Festschrifts, retirement dinners, fiftieth-anniversary parties, and retrospective art shows.

nodes.title: Environmental Communication
nodes.description: Survey of the communication practices found in environment controversies. The sociological aspects of environmental issues will provide background for the investigation of environmental disputes in particular contested areas, such as scientific institutions, communities, workplaces, governments, popular culture, and the media.

nodes.title: Advanced Topics in Mediation and Interaction
nodes.description: Specialized advanced study in mediation and interaction with topics to be determined by the instructor for any given quarter. May be taken three times for credit.

nodes.title: Advanced Topics in Communication
nodes.description: Advanced study of a current topic in the discipline of communication, with topics to be determined by the instructor for any given quarter. Topic and description provided by the department quarterly. May be taken for credit up to three times. Students may receive a combined total of twelve units for COMM 172T and COMM 172TR.

nodes.title: Advanced Topics in Communication
nodes.description: Advanced study of a current topic in the discipline of communication, with topics to be determined by the instructor for any given quarter. Topic and description provided by the department quarterly. This is a distance education course. May be taken for credit up to three times. Students may receive a combined total of twelve units for COMM 172TR and COMM 172T.

nodes.title: Interaction with Technology
nodes.description: In this class we will look closely at the everyday ways in which we interact with technology to discuss sociocultural character of objects, built environments; situated, distributed, and embodied character of knowledges; use of multimodal semiotic resources, talk, gesture, body orientation, and gaze in interaction with technology.

nodes.title: Communication and Social Machines
nodes.description: An examination of the questions that developments in robotics pose to the scholars of communication: How do we communicate when our interlocutors are nonhumans? How do we study objects that are claimed to be endowed with social and affective character?

nodes.title: Cultures of Consumption
nodes.description: This course examines the cultural politics of consumption across time and cultures through several concepts: commodity fetishism; conspicuous consumption; taste; class; and identity formation; consumption’s psychological, phenomenological, and poetic dimensions; and contemporary manifestations of globalization and consumer activism.

nodes.title: Communication and Religion
nodes.description: The secularization thesis—that as society becomes more modern and standards of living rise, the importance of religion will diminish and be confined to the private sphere—may be wrong. We address religion, communication, culture, and politics in the United States.

nodes.title: Culture, Domination, and Resistance
nodes.description: Explores theories and narratives of cultural power, contemporary practices of resistance. Texts from a wide range of disciplines consider how domination is enacted, enforced, and what modes of resistance are employed to contend with uses and abuses of political power.

nodes.title: Communication and Nonhuman Animals
nodes.description: The course increases our awareness of communicative repertoires in nonhuman animals. Noticing their richness allows us to engage topics of iconicity and indexicality, body and movement, feeling and sensation, space and environment, and aspects of voice that do not stand for established units of meaning. We will discuss how this turning to nonhuman communication illuminates human communication and how cross-species communication takes place.

nodes.title: Advanced Studies in Communication Theory
nodes.description: How are messages created, transmitted, and received? What is the relationship between thinking and communicating? How are linguistic processes embedded in sociocultural practices? Course discusses classic texts in the field of communication theory stemming from linguistics, semiotics, philosophy of language, literary theory.

nodes.title: Citizen Consumers
nodes.description: This course considers the idea of the citizen-consumer that organizes much of contemporary urban planning and processes of identity, class, race, and gender formation in cities globally. Focusing on contemporary service oriented economies, we will critically explore how consumption spaces, such as shopping malls, theme parks, plazas, markets, parks, beaches, and tourist resorts, are critical nodes to understand neoliberal patterns of land transformation, labor exploitation, and social change.

nodes.title: Education and Global Citizenship
nodes.description: Concepts, possibilities, and dilemmas inherent in the notion of global citizenship. Formulate goals and instructional strategies for global education, expected competence of individuals within society. Examine roles that communication and curriculum play in the formation of identity, language use, and civic responsibility of global citizens.

nodes.title: Global Economy and Consumer Culture
nodes.description: This course critically examines social and economic forces that shape the making of this new global consumer culture by following the flows of consumption and production between the developed and developing worlds in the 1990s. We will consider how consumers, workers, and citizens participate in a new globalized consumer culture that challenges older distinctions between the First and the Third World. In this course, we will focus on the flows between the United States, Asia, and Latin America.

nodes.title: Global Nature/Global Culture
nodes.description: Considers globalization’s impact on concepts of nature in and through media texts, information systems, circulation of consumer goods and services, the emergence of global brands, science, health initiatives, environmental media activism, technology transfer in the twentieth and early twenty-first centuries.

nodes.title: Communication for Indigenous Justice
nodes.description: The course provides students the opportunity to learn from indigenous scholarship, activism, and art. It introduces students to indigenous justice issues such as knowledge production, environmental stewardship, cultural appropriation, and stereotyped representations—all within the contexts of settler colonialism and indigenous resistance and survival. It gives students tools to examine those issues from communication and media studies perspectives and to explore ways to promote indigenous justice.

nodes.title: Junior Seminar in Communication
nodes.description: The junior seminar enables a detailed examination of a specific topic from the field of communication selected by the instructor, exploring in greater depth theories and methods introduced in the core communication curriculum. Seminars are limited to thirty students with a heavy focus on class participation. Students complete a research project with a significant final product (typically a research paper). No credit for COMM 190 if taken after COMM 190R.

nodes.title: Junior Seminar in Communication
nodes.description: The junior seminar enables a detailed examination of a specific topic from the field of communication selected by the instructor, exploring in greater depth theories and methods introduced in the core communication curriculum. Seminars are limited to thirty students with a heavy focus on class participation. Students complete a research project with a significant final product (typically a research paper). This is a distance education course. No credit for COMM 190R if taken after COMM 190.

nodes.title: Research Seminar in Washington, D.C.
nodes.description: (Same as POLI 194, USP 194, HITO 193, SOCI 194, and COGS 194) Course attached to six-unit internship taken by students participating in the UCDC program. Involves weekly seminar meetings with faculty and teaching assistants and a substantial research paper.

nodes.title: Honors Seminar in Communication I: Methods
nodes.prereq_text: admission to the departmental honors program.

requires.text: admission to the departmental honors program

nodes.description: Preparation of an honors thesis, which can be either a research paper or a media production project. Open to students who have been admitted to the honors program. Grades will be awarded upon completion of the two-quarter sequence.

nodes.title: Honors Seminar in Communication II: Research
nodes.prereq_text: minimum grade of B+ in COMM 196A.
nodes.description: Preparation of an honors thesis, which can be either a research paper or a media production project. Open to students who have been admitted to the honors program. Grades will be awarded upon completion of the two-quarter sequence.

nodes.title: Directed Group Study in Communication
nodes.description: Directed group study on a topic or in a field not included in the regular curriculum by special arrangement with a faculty member. May be taken three times for credit.

nodes.title: Independent Study in Communication
nodes.description: Independent study and research under the direction of a member of the faculty. May be taken three times for credit.

nodes.title: Honors Project Completion
nodes.description: Under the guidance of both Honors Seminar director and faculty mentor, students will complete their thesis or media production and prepare for a presentation of their finished product at a public event sponsored by the department.

nodes.title: Dimensions of Culture: Diversity
nodes.prereq_text: satisfaction of UC Entry Level Writing Requirement or concurrent enrollment in AWP 3, Analytical Writing.

requires.text: satisfaction of UC Entry Level Writing Requirement in AWP 3

nodes.description: This course focuses on sociocultural diversity in examining class, ethnicity, race, gender, and sexuality as significant markers of differences among persons. Emphasizing American society while cultivating students’ critical reading skills, it explores the cultural understandings of diversity and its economic, moral, and political consequences. Restrictions: Marshall College students only, must be taken for a letter grade.

nodes.title: Dimensions of Culture: Justice
nodes.prereq_text: satisfaction of UC Entry Level Writing Requirement and completion of DOC 1. Enrollment by department approval only.

items.text: satisfaction of UC Entry Level Writing Requirement

nodes.description: This course considers the nature of justice in philosophical, historical, and legal terms. Topics include racial justice, political representation, economic justice, gender and justice, the rights of cultural minorities, and crime and punishment. The course offers intensive instruction in writing university-level expository prose, specifically thesis-based argumentative essays. Restrictions: Marshall College students only, must be taken for a letter grade.

nodes.title: Design of Everyday Things
nodes.description: A project-based course examining how principles from cognitive science apply to the design of things simple (doors) and complex (new technology). Learn about affordances, constraints, mappings, and conceptual models. Learn observational and design skills. Become a human-centered design thinker.

nodes.title: Introduction to Environmental Systems
nodes.description: This course explores the interdisciplinary character of environmental issues through an examination of a particular topic (climate change, for example) from numerous disciplinary perspectives (e.g., biology, chemistry, physics, political science, and economics).

nodes.title: Introduction to Global Health
nodes.description: Provides a foundational interdisciplinary understanding of complex global health issues and introduces major concepts and principles in global health. The course surveys the range of problems contributing to the global burden of disease and disability including infectious disease, mental illness, refugee and immigrant health, natural disasters, climate change, and food insecurity.

nodes.title: Introduction to Political Science: American Politics
nodes.description: This course surveys the processes and institutions of American politics. Among the topics discussed are individual political attitudes and values, political participation, voting, parties, interest groups, Congress, presidency, Supreme Court, the federal bureaucracy, and domestic and foreign policy making. POLI 10 is Lecture only, and POLI 10D is Lecture plus Discussion section. These courses are equivalents of each other in regard to major requirements, and students may not receive credit for both 10 and 10D.

nodes.title: Introduction to Political Science: American Politics
nodes.description: This course surveys the processes and institutions of American politics. Among the topics discussed are individual political attitudes and values, political participation, voting, parties, interest groups, Congress, presidency, Supreme Court, the federal bureaucracy, and domestic and foreign policy making. POLI 10 is Lecture only, and POLI 10D is Lecture plus Discussion section. These courses are equivalents of each other in regard to major requirements, and students may not receive credit for both 10 and 10D.

nodes.title: Introduction to Law and Society
nodes.description: This course is designed as a broad introduction to the study of law as a social institution and its relations to other institutions in society. The focus will be less on the substance of law (legal doctrine and judicial opinions) than on the process of law–how legal rules both reflect and shape basic social values and their relation to social, political, and economic conflicts within society.

nodes.title: History of US Urban Communities
nodes.description: This course charts the development of urban communities across the United States both temporally and geographically. It examines the patterns of cleavage, conflict, convergence of interest, and consensus that have structured urban life. Social, cultural, and economic forces will be analyzed for the roles they have played in shaping the diverse communities of America’s cities.

nodes.title: Introduction to Media
nodes.prereq_text: none. Open to visual arts and cinematic arts majors and minors.

requires.text: Open to visual arts and cinematic arts majors and minors

nodes.description: Operating as both a lecture and production course, this introductory class provides a technical foundation and theoretical context for all subsequent production-oriented film and video studies. In the laboratory, the student will learn the basic skills necessary to initiate video production. Completion of Visual Arts 70N is necessary to obtain a media card. Program or materials fees may apply.
